newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Waxing Taiwan recovery seen easing '97 joblessness.
newsitem.headline: Waxing Taiwan recovery seen easing '97 joblessness.

text.p: With Taiwan's economic recovery apparently gathering steam, officials and economists said on Monday the island's jobless rate in 1997 was likely to slip to around 2.5 percent.

The government on Monday disclosed that January joblessness was 2.68 percent, slightly higher than the average forecast of 2.56 percent that resulted from a February 21 Reuters Poll of Taiwan economists.
The rate averaged 2.60 percent in 1996, the highest since it clocked 2.66 percent in 1986, according to the cabinet's Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics.
In December, the rate was at 2.60 percent, an improvement over November's 2.86 percent and well below the 10-year monthly high of 3.19 percent set in August.
"Because of the recovering economy, we could expect falling unemployment in 1997," said Cheng Shuo-liang, a section chief at the statistics directorate, told Reuters.
"But it's not easy to see the rate approaching 2.0 percent. It should be around 2.5 percent this year," he said.

The directorate last week raised its forecast for Taiwan's 1997 gross domestic product growth to 6.28 percent from 6.20 percent, an adjustment reflecting the higher-than-expected 5.71 percent GDP growth for all of 1996 and a consistent uptrend.
Taiwan's GDP growth started at just 5.12 percent in the first quarter of 1996, then improved steadily to 5.42, 5.61 and 6.62 percent in the following quarters.
Economists said the recovery should have a particularly noticeable impact on job creation in the second half.
"As the jobless rate is a lagging indicator, we should not expect an immediate fall in the early stage of an economic recovery," said National Securities economist Lin Kuo-yang.
"But in the second half, we should be able to see a gradual rise in employment and a fall in unemployment," he said.
Unemployment would fall because of slowing plant closures, while Taiwan's political season would create new, if short-lived, jobs late in 1997, said Nomura Securities economist Amy Huang.
"Temporary employment for campaign needs in the year-end local goverment elections should increase to help the jobless rate lower," Huang said.
National Securities expects full-year 1997 joblessness to come in at 2.4 percent, while Nomura is forecasting 2.5 percent.
Officials attributed the slightly higher-than-expected January jobless rate to a decline in student internships at a time when students were focusing on semester-end exams.

In the Reuters Poll, economists said joblessness should ease in January from December because Taiwan enterprises usually pay bonuses days before the Chinese New Year, which fell this year on February 7. A worker planning to change jobs was highly unlikely to resign before receiving a year-end bonus.
Cheng of the statistics agency explained that this timing factor was less significant this year because of a relatively high rate of plant closures.
Taiwan's jobless rate held close to 1.5 percent in 1991-1994 but rose to 1.79 percent in 1995 and pushed above three percent in August, September and October 1996.

Officials had attributed the shift to higher jobless levels to a fundamental change in Taiwan's economy -- a move toward service-oriented industries from labour-intensive manufacturing that had engendered decades of dramatic economic development.
